concepts.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way to make complex visual modeling computations tractable.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way that allows us to reason about the visual world even when we're modeling very complicated situations. These models are useful in vision, where we often need to exploit modularity to make computations tractable.
concepts.motivation_md: They provide a formal framework to handle uncertainty and complexity in computer vision by breaking down large problems into smaller, interacting components.
concepts.recap_md:
- Represent joint probability distributions using modular structures.
- Enable tractable computation in complex modeling scenarios.
- Widely used in computer vision for reasoning about the visual world.

concepts.title: Likelihood Term
concepts.one_liner: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.content: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In Bayesian inference, the likelihood term is essential for modeling the forward process of how hidden states or scenes produce the data we actually observe.
concepts.recap_md: - The likelihood $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ models the generation of observations from a scene.

concepts.title: Prior Probability
concepts.one_liner: The prior probability, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.content: The prior probability, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring. For inference, we often ignore the denominator in Bayes' rule as it is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: Prior probabilities allow us to incorporate existing knowledge or beliefs about which states of the world are more likely before any data is observed.
concepts.recap_md: - The prior $p(\mathbf{x})$ represents the probability of a scene occurring before considering observations.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.one_liner: The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the denominator in Bayes' rule and is constant with respect to the variables being estimated.
concepts.content: The denominator $P(\mathbf{y})$ is called the evidence. It is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate, $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The evidence acts as a normalization constant in Bayes' rule, ensuring that the posterior probability distribution sums to one.
concepts.recap_md: - The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the marginal probability of the observations.

concepts.title: Point Estimate
concepts.one_liner: A point estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is a single best estimate for a hidden variable $\mathbf{x}$ derived from the posterior probability.
concepts.content: Typically, we make many observations, $\mathbf{y}$, of the variables of some system, and we want to find the state of some hidden variable, $\mathbf{x}$, given those observations. The posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$, tells us the probability for any value of the hidden variables, $\mathbf{x}$. From this posterior probability, we often want some single best estimate for $\mathbf{x}$, denoted $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ and called a point estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: While a posterior distribution provides a full range of probabilities, practical applications often require a single concrete value to act upon.
concepts.recap_md: - A point estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is a single value chosen to represent the most likely or best state of a hidden variable.

concepts.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)
concepts.one_liner: The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$.
concepts.content: Selecting the best estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ requires specifying a penalty for making a wrong guess. If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})$. This is because any other explanation $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ for the observations $\mathbf{y}$ would be less probable. This value is called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: The MAP estimate is used when we want the most probable single explanation for our data, effectively treating all incorrect guesses as equally bad.
concepts.recap_md: - The MAP estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is the mode of the posterior distribution.

key_passage.text: That is called the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.

motivation.text: If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of x that maximizes the posterior probability, p(x | y) (because any other explanation x̂ for the observations y would be less probable).

concepts.title: Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE)
concepts.one_liner: The minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate is the point estimate that minimizes the average squared distance from the correct answer.
concepts.content: If we want to penalize wrong answers as a function of how far they are from the correct answer, specifically using the squared distance in $\mathbf{x}$, then the point estimate that minimizes the average value of that error is called the minimum mean squared error estimate (MMSE). To find this estimate, we seek the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that minimizes the squared error, weighted by the probability of each outcome: $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \mbox{argmin}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \int_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}})' (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) d\mathbf{x}$$ Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ to solve for the stationary point, the global minimum for this convex function, we find $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) d\mathbf{x}.$$ Thus, the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE}$, is the mean of the posterior distribution. If $\mathbf{x}$ represents a discretized space, then the marginalization integrals over $d\mathbf{x}$ become sums over the corresponding discrete states of $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The MMSE estimate is ideal when large errors are significantly more costly than small ones, leading to an estimate that represents the average expected value.
concepts.recap_md: - The MMSE estimate is the mean of the posterior distribution.

concepts.title: Marginal Probability for Discrete Variables
concepts.one_liner: For discrete variables, the marginal probability at a node is computed by summing over the states of all other nodes.
concepts.content: For the case of discrete variables, we compute the marginal probability at a node by summing over the states at all the other nodes, $$p\left(x_i \mid \mathbf{y}\right)=\sum_{\lambda_i} \sum_{x_j} p\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N \mid \mathbf{y}\right),$$ where the notation $j \backslash i$ means "all possible values of $j$ except for $j = i$."
concepts.motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to focus on the probability distribution of a specific variable of interest by removing the influence of other variables in a joint distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal probability for a discrete node is found by summing the joint probability over all other variables.

concepts.title: Messages

position.section_title: Simple Example of Inference in a Graphical Model

concepts.one_liner: Messages are partial sums that pass information between nodes in a probabilistic graphical model.
concepts.content: Partial sums are named messages because they pass information from one node to another. For example, the message from node 3 to node 2 is defined as $m_{32}(x_2) = \sum_{x_3} \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) m_{63}(x_3)$. Another example is the message from node 2 to node 1: $m_{21}(x_1) = \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) m_{52}(x_2) m_{32}(x_2)$. Note that the messages are always about the states of the node that the message is being sent to; that is, the arguments of the message $m_{ij}$ are the states $x_j$ of node $j$. The algorithm corresponding to these calculations is called belief propagation.
concepts.motivation_md: Messages provide a computationally efficient way to perform inference in complex graphical models by breaking down global sums into local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages $m_{ij}$ pass information from node $i$ to node $j$ regarding the states of node $j$.

concepts.title: Graph
concepts.one_liner: A probabilistic graphical model is a graph that describes a class of probability distributions sharing a common structure.
concepts.content: A probabilistic graphical model is a graph that describes a class of probability distributions sharing a common structure. The graph has nodes, drawn as circles, indicating the variables of the joint probability. It has edges, drawn as lines connecting nodes to other nodes. In undirected graphical models, the edges are line segments without arrowheads.
concepts.motivation_md: Graphical models provide a visual and mathematical language to represent complex dependencies between many variables, allowing us to reason about joint probability distributions through their structural properties.
concepts.recap_md:
- Nodes represent variables in a joint probability distribution.
 - Edges represent connections or dependencies between variables.
 - Undirected edges indicate a lack of specific causal direction in the relationship.

concepts.title: Undirected Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: In undirected graphical models, edges indicate the conditional independence structure of the nodes.
concepts.content: In undirected graphical models, the edges indicate the conditional independence structure of the nodes of the graph. If there is no edge between two nodes, then the variables described by those nodes are independent, conditioned on the values of intervening nodes in any path between them in the graph. If two nodes do have a line between them, then we cannot assume they are independent.
concepts.motivation_md: Undirected models are useful for representing symmetric relationships where variables constrain each other without a clear parent-child or causal hierarchy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Missing edges imply conditional independence between variables.
 - Existing edges indicate that independence cannot be assumed.
 - Independence is conditioned on the values of intervening nodes in a path.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Belief propagation is an algorithm that exploits the structure of a joint probability to perform inference efficiently.
concepts.content:
Belief propagation (BP) is an algorithm used to estimate the states of unobserved variables given a probabilistic graphical model and observations. It exploits the model's structure to avoid exponential growth in computation. By substituting the joint probability into the marginalization equation, we see that not every variable is coupled to every other one:

$$p(x_1 \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \sum_{x_2} \sum_{x_3} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$$

We can pass summations through variables they don't sum over, reorganizing the calculation:

$$\begin{aligned} p\left(x_1 \mid \mathbf{y}\right) &= \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \sum_{x_3} \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3) \end{aligned}$$

This factorization reduces the computational complexity for a chain of length $N$ from order $|x|^N$ to order $(N-1)|x|^2$, representing a shift from exponential to linear dependence on $N$. The partial sums are called messages because they pass information between nodes. For example, a message $m_{ij}(x_j)$ contains information about the states of the node it is being sent to. The algorithm stores and reuses these messages to find marginal probabilities at different nodes optimally.
concepts.motivation_md: Directly calculating marginal probabilities in large models is computationally impossible due to exponential complexity; belief propagation makes this feasible by using the distributive law to factorize sums.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reduces computational complexity from exponential to linear in chain-like structures.
 - Uses "messages" to pass information about variable states between nodes.
 - Efficiently computes marginal probabilities by storing and reusing partial sums.

The other partial sum is the message from node 2 to node 1, $m_{21}(x_1) = \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) m_{52}(x_2) m_{32}(x_2)$. concepts.title: Hammersley-Clifford Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem states that a positive probability distribution's independence structure is defined by the product of functions over its maximal cliques.
concepts.content:
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem specifies the form the joint probability must have for any given graphical model. It states that a positive probability distribution has the independence structure described by a graphical model if and only if it can be written as a product of functions over the variables of each maximal clique:

$$p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \prod_{x_c \in x_i} \Psi_{c} (x_c),$$

where the product is over all maximal cliques $x_c$ in the graph. For a graph where the maximal cliques are $(x_1, x_2)$ and $(x_2, x_3)$, the joint probability must be a product of functions of these specific cliques.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the fundamental link between the topology of a graph and the algebraic factorization of its corresponding probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md:
- Relates graph structure to the factorization of the joint probability distribution.
 - Requires the distribution to be strictly positive.
 - The joint probability is expressed as a product of functions over maximal cliques.

concepts.title: Clique
concepts.one_liner: A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique.
concepts.content:
A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique. These graphs illustrate the clique property:

![A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the same clique.](figures/graphical_models/cliques1.png){width="50%" #fig-chain}

concepts.title: Markov Chain
concepts.one_liner: A Markov chain is a sequence of variables where, conditional on the present, the future is independent of the past.
concepts.content:
A Markov chain structure consists of variables forming a linear sequence. In a model with observed variables $y_i$ and unobserved variables $x_i$:

(see figure: Same three-node Markov chain of @fig-chain.)

This is a Markov chain structure because the hidden variables have the Markov property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all variables shown here is $p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) = \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Markov chains simplify the modeling of sequential data (like time series or text) by assuming that only the current state affects the next state, drastically reducing the number of parameters needed.
concepts.recap_md:
- Variables are arranged in a linear sequence.
 - Satisfies the Markov property: the future is independent of the past given the present state.
 - The joint probability factorizes into local interactions between adjacent nodes.

concepts.title: Directed Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions.
concepts.content:
Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating arrows pointing into it. For example, this graph

(see figure: A directed graphical model with three variables.)

denotes the joint probability:
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_2) p(x_1 \bigm | x_2) p(x_3 \bigm | x_2)$$

The general rule for writing the joint probability described by a directed graph is that each node $x_n$ contributes the factor $p(x_n \bigm | x_{\Xi})$, where $\Xi$ is the set of nodes with arrows pointing in to node $x_n$. Directed graphical models are often used to describe causal processes.
concepts.motivation_md: Directed models are ideal for representing causal relationships and generative processes where one variable directly influences another in a specific direction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Edges represent directed dependencies (arrows).
 - The joint probability is a product of conditional probabilities.
 - Each node is conditioned on its "parents" (nodes with arrows pointing to it).

concepts.title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models and neural networks share graph structures but differ fundamentally in what their nodes, edges, and computations represent.
concepts.content:
The probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) and neural networks (NNs) share a graph structure with nodes and edges, but these components mean different things in each case. In a NN diagram, nodes typically represent real-valued scalar activations, whereas in a PGM, nodes represent random variables (real or discrete, scalar or vector). Edges in PGMs determine statistical dependencies, while edges in NNs determine which values are involved in a linear summation to the next layer.

The primary difference lies in what they calculate. PGMs represent factorized probability distributions and pass messages to compute probabilities, such as the marginal probability at a node. In contrast, NNs compute results that minimize an expected loss or an energy function. This goal of minimizing loss rather than calculating a probability allows for more general computations, though the output may be less modular or interpretable because it does not represent a probability. Both PGMs and NNs can organize nodes into grid-like structures or arbitrary graphs.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinction between PGMs and NNs is crucial for choosing the right framework for a task. PGMs excel at interpretable probabilistic reasoning and handling uncertainty, while NNs provide a more flexible, general-purpose framework for optimization and learning from large-scale data.
concepts.recap_md: - PGMs represent statistical dependencies and compute probabilities via message passing.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message
concepts.one_liner: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$ from node $i$ to node $j$ is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree leaving node $i$ that excludes node $j$.
concepts.content: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is defined as the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
concepts.motivation_md: In graphical models, calculating marginal probabilities directly is often computationally expensive. Belief propagation messages serve as partial sums that allow for efficient, local computation of these marginals by summarizing information from subtrees.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}$ represents the summarized probability information from the subtree rooted at $i$ (excluding $j$).

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message Update Rule
aliases: recursive belief propagation message update rule
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation update rule computes messages by multiplying incoming messages with pairwise compatibility functions and marginalizing over the sending node's states.
concepts.content:
The belief propagation message update rule is derived by passing summations over node states through nodes that are constant over those summations, resulting in a recursive factorization. As illustrated in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.), messages such as $m_{j+1,j}$ and $m_{kj}$ correspond to partial sums over specific nodes in the graph. Marginalization over the states of all nodes leaving node $j$, not including node $i$, leads to the belief propagation message passing rule.

To compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

1. Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node $j$, except for the message from node $i$ back to node $j$.
2. Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function $\psi_{ij}(x_i, x_j)$.
3. Marginalize over the variable $x_j$.

These steps are summarized in the following equation to compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

$$m_{j i}\left(x_i\right)=\sum_{x_j} \psi_{i i}\left(x_i, x_j\right) \prod_{k \in \eta(j) \backslash i} m_{k j}\left(x_j\right)$$

where $\eta(j) \backslash i$ denotes the neighbors of node $j$ except for node $i$. (see figure: Pictorial depiction of belief propagation message passing rules of equation (@eq-bpupdate), where $\odot$ indicates elementwise multiplication (i.e., the Hadamard product).) Any local potential functions $\phi_{j}(x_j)$ are treated as an additional message into node $j$, such that $m_{0j}(x_j) = \phi_{j}(x_j)$. For continuous variables, the sum over the states of $x_j$ is replaced by an integral over the domain of $x_j$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule allows for the recursive calculation of marginals in a tree-structured graph by breaking down a global summation into local, modular computations that can be passed between neighbors.
concepts.recap_md: - To send a message to node $i$, node $j$ combines all incoming messages from its other neighbors with its local compatibility function.

motivation.text: Remembering that the message from node j to node i is the sum over the tree leaving node j, we can then read-off the recursive belief propagation message update rule by marginalizing over the state probabilities at node j.

concepts.title: Nosey Neighbor Rule
concepts.one_liner: The 'nosey neighbor rule' describes how BP messages represent a neighbor's belief about a node's state based on all the information they have gathered.
concepts.content: Belief propagation messages are partial sums in the marginalization calculation, where the arguments of messages are always the state of the node that the message is going to. This follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (from Brendan Frey, Univ. Toronto): Every node is a house in some neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor provides an intuitive way to understand the directionality and content of messages in the belief propagation algorithm.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages are always functions of the state of the receiving node.

concepts.title: Marginal Probability in Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: In a loopless network, the marginal probability at a node is the product of all its incoming messages.
concepts.content:
(see figure: To compute the marginal probability at node $i$, we multiply together all the incoming messages at that node: $p_{i}$ as another message.)

The marginal probability at a node $i$ is the sum over the joint probabilities of all states except those of $x_i$. In a network with no loops, the conditional independence structure ensures that the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$. Because the subtrees are independent when conditioned on node $i$, the marginal probability is simply the product of all incoming messages:

$$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)}  m_{ji}(x_i)$$

This product includes the local clique potential at node $i$, $\psi_i(x_i)$, which is treated as one of the incoming messages.
concepts.motivation_md: The primary goal of belief propagation is to compute these marginal probabilities efficiently without performing an exhaustive summation over the entire joint distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - The marginal probability $p_i(x_i)$ is the product of all messages $m_{ji}(x_i)$ entering node $i$.

concepts.title: Message Update Protocols
concepts.one_liner: Message update protocols like depth-first and parallel updates determine the sequence in which belief propagation messages are calculated across a network.
concepts.content:
To find all messages, the recursive BP update rule is applied whenever all required incoming messages are defined. The process starts at leaf nodes, which can send messages because they have no incoming messages other than from the recipient node. Two natural protocols are used:

1. **Depth-first update**: One node is chosen as the root. Messages are passed from the leaves up to the root, and then back down from the root to the leaves.
2. **Parallel update**: At each step, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has already received the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:05fcd402b5e6435d]
[FIGURE:642603864966b118]
[FIGURE:8a28a6db9b463c3e]
**Synchronous parallel update schedule**: Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages.

[FIGURE:25f610399a220f05]
[FIGURE:9560b6515cfb38e6]
[FIGURE:455ef9a295437c12]
[FIGURE:a33008ecd7f522ba]
**Depth-first BP message passing schedule**: Select a root node, start at leaves, proceed to root, perform an outgoing sweep, and end at leaf nodes.

A single sweep through all nodes allows the calculation of the marginal at any node. A second sweep (from root back to leaves) calculates all messages needed for marginals at every node, requiring only twice the computation of a single-node marginal.
concepts.motivation_md: Efficiently computing marginals for all nodes in a graph requires a systematic way to order message updates so that dependencies are met and computations are reused.
concepts.recap_md: - Depth-first updates use a root-based two-pass sweep (leaves-to-root and root-to-leaves).

key_passage.text: Two natural message passing protocols are consistent with that rule: depth-first update, and parallel update. In depth-first update, one node is arbitrarily picked as the root. Messages are then passed from the leaves of the tree (leaves, relative to that root node) up to the root, then back down to the leaves. In parallel update, at each turn, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received all the necessary incoming messages.

concepts.title: Loopy Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Loopy belief propagation applies standard BP update rules to graphs with cycles, often providing useful local approximations despite the lack of global guarantees.
concepts.content:
The BP message update rules provide exact marginals only when the network topology is a tree or a chain. For graphs with loops, exact computation depends on the treewidth, which can be intractably large in fields like computer vision. However, applying BP update rules locally as a heuristic is often effective. This is known as the **loopy belief propagation algorithm**:

1. Convert the graph to pairwise potentials.
2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1.
3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.
concepts.motivation_md: Many real-world problems, such as image processing, involve graphs with many loops where exact inference is impossible; loopy BP provides a practical, though approximate, alternative.
concepts.recap_md: - Loopy BP is a heuristic that applies tree-based update rules to cyclic graphs.

key_passage.text: Here is the algorithm, also know as loopy belief propagation algorithm: 1. Convert graph to pairwise potentials. 2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1. 3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.

motivation.text: Message update rules are described locally, and one might imagine that it is a useful local operation to perform, even without the global guarantees of ordinary BP. It turns out that is true.

concepts.title: Treewidth
concepts.one_liner: Treewidth is a graph-theoretic quantity that determines the complexity of exact marginal probability computation in graphs with loops.
concepts.content: The BP message update rules only work to give the exact marginals when the topology of the network is that of a tree or a chain. In general, exact computation of marginal probabilities for graphs with loops depends on a graph-theoretic quantity known as the **treewidth** of the graph.

concepts.title: Max-Product Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Max-product belief propagation is a variation of the BP algorithm that finds the state configuration maximizing the joint probability.
concepts.content: Instead of summing over the states of other nodes, we are sometimes interested in finding the configuration $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the joint probability. Because the argmax operator passes through constant variables in the same way the summation sign does, an alternate version of the BP algorithm can be used. In this **max-product** version of belief propagation, the summation in the update rule is replaced with an argmax. This algorithm computes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate of the hidden states.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard BP finds marginal probabilities, max-product BP is used when the goal is to find the single most likely global state of the system.

prereq.rationale: Belief propagation exploits the factorized form of the joint probability, which is guaranteed by the Hammersley-Clifford theorem.
Belief propagation is an algorithm used to estimate variable states given a probabilistic graphical model.
The theorem states that the joint probability is a product of functions over the variables of each maximal clique.
The theorem specifies the necessary form of the joint probability for a distribution to match an undirected graphical model's structure.
A clique is a specific set of nodes within a graph structure.
A maximal clique is defined as a clique that cannot include more nodes without losing the clique property.
The definition of directed graphical models relies on the graph structure where nodes represent variables and arrows represent dependencies.
This concept defines the specific graph-based structure (nodes and edges) that constitutes a probabilistic graphical model.
Undirected models are a specific type of graphical model where the edges lack direction, defining a specific interpretation of the graph structure.
The likelihood term p(y|x) is a fundamental component of directed graphical models where x is a parent of y.
Calculating the MAP estimate requires the posterior probability, which is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior.
Marginal probability calculation is a standard operation performed on nodes within probabilistic graphical models.
Belief propagation is the algorithm defined by the exchange of these messages to perform inference.
Messages are the fundamental mechanism for passing information between nodes within the PGM framework.
The definition of messages uses potential functions (Ε), which are the core components of undirected graphical models.
Belief propagation messages are a specific implementation of the general message-passing concept in graphical models.
The update rule defines how belief propagation messages are recursively calculated from other messages.
The update rule is derived by passing summations (marginalization) over node states through the graph.
In belief propagation, the marginal probability at a node is computed as the product of all its incoming messages.
This technique provides a specific algorithm to compute the general definition of marginal probability for discrete variables.
Protocols like depth-first or parallel updates determine the sequence in which the recursive BP update rule is applied.
Loopy BP applies the standard belief propagation update rules to graphs with cycles.
Loopy BP is used as a heuristic when the treewidth of a graph is too large for exact computation.
Treewidth is a graph-theoretic property used to analyze the complexity of inference in undirected graphical models.
Max-product BP is an alternate version of the standard belief propagation algorithm.
The max-product algorithm is specifically designed to compute the MAP estimate.
Comparing PGMs to neural networks requires a foundational understanding of what PGMs are and their graphical nature.
The text contrasts the message-passing nature of PGM computation with the loss-minimization nature of NNs.

overlay.rationale: The text demonstrates the belief propagation algorithm's efficiency by applying it to a three-node Markov chain example.
A Markov chain is a specific linear topology of an undirected graphical model.
Directed graphical models are a specific class of probabilistic graphical models that use directed acyclic graphs to represent factorizations.
Directed models factorize into conditional probabilities based on parent nodes, whereas undirected models use potential functions over cliques.
A Markov chain is a simple, linear directed graphical model where each node has exactly one parent (the previous state).
The MAP estimate is a specific type of point estimate that selects the value with the highest posterior probability.
The MMSE estimate is a specific type of point estimate that minimizes the average squared distance from the correct answer.
MAP and MMSE are two different strategies for choosing a point estimate based on different penalty functions for wrong guesses.
The summation of messages is used to compute marginal probabilities in discrete graphical models.
The 'nosey neighbor rule' provides an intuitive metaphor for what a belief propagation message represents conceptually.
Loopy BP is the application of the general belief propagation algorithm to graphs containing loops.
Standard BP computes marginal probabilities via summation, while max-product BP uses argmax to find the most likely configuration.
The concept highlights how nodes and edges in PGMs represent random variables and statistical dependencies, unlike their counterparts in NNs.
